title: 7 Classroom Management Strategies To Get Your Class Back On Track
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin offers seven quick 'reset' strategies for the inevitable days when a class becomes unfocused and unmanageable regardless of cause. These include sprinting outside or in the gym to release nervous energy, physically 'redoing' the school day by walking students back outside and restarting the entry routine, playing a fun activity like capture the flag, taking a short yoga or exercise break, practicing a minute of silence with belly breathing, re-modeling an expected routine in detail, and letting students informally socialize for five minutes via a 'say-hello' strategy. He advises against explaining or lecturing why the strategy is being used—teachers should simply announce the activity and proceed. Over time, Linsin says, teachers develop a feel for which of the seven strategies best fits a given moment of restlessness or disengagement.
points: Use physical exercise, such as sprinting outside or a short yoga/calisthenics break, to calm nervous energy and refocus a squirrelly class.
Physically 'redo' the school day by walking students back outside and restarting entry routines with clear, simple reminders.
Use a minute of silence combined with belly breathing to lower stress and redirect student attention.
Re-model an expected routine in detail as a refresher when students seem to have forgotten classroom expectations.
Announce a reset strategy directly without lecturing or explaining why it's being used—just do it and move on.
quotes: Whatever it is, there are times when your class just can’t seem to get it together. They’re unfocused, squirrelly, prone to misbehavior.
Take your students outside or to the school gym, line them up on the end line of the basketball court, and run.
Have your students grab their backpacks, jackets, and lunches, walk them outside the classroom, and start your day over again.
Use the one-minute of silence strategy followed by belly breathing. This sends oxygen to the brain, lowers blood pressure, and calms the mind.
Don’t give your students an explanation of why you’re using any of these back-on-track classroom management strategies. Don’t lecture them or tell them how awful they are. Just do it.
With experience, you’ll get a feel for what your students need and when, and you’ll be able to dial it up in a hurry.
